```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 100)
```

Can the strongest edges and most prominent nodes in a psychological network be
trusted to remain similar in another sample? Consider a network of
self-efficacy, learning strategies and test anxiety, in which the constructs are
nodes and their estimated associations are edges. In a partial correlation
network, each edge describes an association adjusted for the other variables,
while centrality measures summarise aspects of each node's position. These tools
allow researchers to explore multivariate patterns rather than examine every
construct in isolation (Borsboom et al., 2021). Yet the interpretation of edge
weights and centrality depends on the estimation method and available data,
making stability and reliability important considerations (Isvoranu & Epskamp,
2023).

Network methods have been used in education to study the relationships among
learning processes and how these relationships vary across contexts and time.
Saqr et al. (2024) introduce psychological networks as an approach to analysing
learning and complex learning processes. Applications include networks of
students' monitoring events across phases of regulation (Malmberg et al.,
2022) and the temporal dynamics of self-regulation during academic writing
(Saqr et al., 2021). These studies illustrate the value of examining patterns
of relationships, but an apparent connection or prominent node in an estimated
network should not automatically be treated as a reproducible finding.

A network fitted to one sample will generally differ from a network fitted
to another sample from the same population. Consequently, applied researchers
need to assess uncertainty in individual edge weights, whether nodes can be
distinguished in centrality, and how much the network changes when observations
are omitted or divided into groups. Resampling provides an empirical way to
investigate these questions by repeatedly estimating networks from the
available observations (Epskamp et al., 2018). Assessing and clearly reporting
such uncertainty is also part of good practice in cross-sectional network
analysis (Burger et al., 2023). These checks describe the robustness of an
estimated network; they do not establish causal relationships or guarantee
replication in a new population.

This article demonstrates five complementary diagnostics in `psychnets`:
bootstrap intervals for edges and centrality, bootstrap comparisons of nodes,
case-dropping stability of centrality, case-dropping reliability of edge
weights, and split-half reliability. The worked example uses questionnaire
responses generated by a large language model, rather than observations of
students, and therefore illustrates methods rather than substantive findings
about learners. For each diagnostic, we explain the question it addresses,
show the relevant output, and discuss what researchers can reasonably report.
The functions use a consistent network-estimation interface, allowing the
same workflow to be used with other estimators.

```{r setup}
library(psychnets)
set.seed(1)
```

Because the procedures involve random resampling, setting the seed makes the
illustrative results reproducible.

## Data

`SRL_Claude` contains 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for
Learning Questionnaire generated by the large language model Claude for a
study of responses to psychological surveys (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). The
model-generated responses are unusually internally consistent and produce
several large estimated edges. They make the numerical examples easy to
inspect, but do not provide evidence about relationships among constructs in
real students.

- **Nodes:** five construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7: `CSU` (cognitive
  strategy use), `IV` (intrinsic value), `SE` (self-efficacy), `SR`
  (self-regulation) and `TA` (test anxiety).
- **Observations:** one row per respondent; the data are complete.

```{r data}
head(SRL_Claude)
```

The main analyses use an EBIC graphical lasso (`method = "glasso"`) to
estimate a regularised network of partial correlations. All five diagnostics
therefore assess the same type of fitted network.

## How precise is each edge?

`net_boot()` draws samples of observations with replacement, estimates a
network for each sample and summarises the resulting edge weights. The output
provides each observed weight, the bootstrap mean, a 95% percentile interval
and the proportion of resamples in which the edge has a non-zero estimate.
The `significant` flag indicates that the percentile interval excludes zero;
it should not be read as proof of an underlying relationship. For substantive
research, at least 1,000 bootstrap samples provide a more useful basis for
assessing precision. Here, 200 resamples keep the demonstration manageable.

```{r boot}
b <- net_boot(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", n_boot = 200, cores = 1)
b
as.data.frame(b)
```

Eight of the ten edges have percentile intervals that exclude zero, and
all eight are selected in every bootstrap sample. The largest positive
edge, `CSU`–`SR`, has an observed weight of 0.73 and an interval from 0.65
to 0.77. By contrast, `CSU`–`IV` has a weight of 0.002, an interval from
0 to 0.12 and a non-zero estimate in 55% of resamples. The `IV`–`TA`
edge has a weight of -0.014, an interval from -0.13 to 0.02 and a
non-zero estimate in 75.5% of resamples. The latter two intervals include
zero, so these data do not support confident interpretation of those edges.
The plot presents the edge estimates alongside their intervals, ordered by
weight:

```{r boot-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(b)
```

## How precise is each node's centrality?

The bootstrap samples also provide intervals for node centrality. Strength
is the sum of the absolute weights of a node's edges, whereas expected
influence sums signed edge weights. This distinction matters when the network
contains both positive and negative associations.

```{r boot-centrality}
as.data.frame(b, what = "centrality")
plot(b, type = "centrality")
```

Self-regulation (`SR`) has the highest observed strength, 1.95, with a
bootstrap interval from 1.83 to 2.03. This interval does not overlap the
interval of any other node. Intrinsic value (`IV`) has the lowest observed
strength, 0.99, with an interval from 0.83 to 1.27. The intervals for
cognitive strategy use, self-efficacy and test anxiety overlap, so their
ranking cannot be inferred from separate intervals alone. Expected influence
answers a different question: self-efficacy and test anxiety have negative
values (-0.37 and -0.33), reflecting the balance of their signed edges.
The next analysis compares strengths directly.

## Which nodes can be ranked?

`difference_test()` compares the centralities of pairs of nodes or the
weights of pairs of edges. It calculates each difference across the existing
bootstrap samples, then reports its percentile interval and a two-sided
bootstrap p-value. The stored samples from `net_boot()` are reused rather
than fitted again. For the ten pairwise strength comparisons, `p_adjust = "BH"`
applies a false discovery rate adjustment to the p-values (Benjamini &
Hochberg, 1995). An interval containing zero indicates that the bootstrap
differences do not clearly distinguish the pair.

```{r difference}
difference_test(b, type = "strength", p_adjust = "BH")
```

Nine of the ten comparisons have intervals excluding zero and are flagged
as significant in the output. Self-regulation has greater strength than every
other node, with adjusted p-values reported as 0 for these comparisons at
the available bootstrap resolution. Cognitive strategy use also exceeds
self-efficacy and test anxiety (adjusted p = 0.044 for each comparison).
The only pair not distinguished is self-efficacy and test anxiety: their
observed difference is -0.12, with an interval from -0.33 to 0.08 and an
adjusted p-value of 0.26. Thus, self-regulation can be placed first and
intrinsic value last in this example, but the evidence does not establish
an ordering between self-efficacy and test anxiety.

## Is the centrality ranking stable when cases are dropped?

`net_stability()` re-estimates the network on random subsets that drop an
increasing proportion of the respondents and correlates the centralities of
each subset with those of the full sample. The correlation-stability
coefficient (CS-coefficient) is the largest proportion of cases that can be
dropped while the correlation stays at or above 0.7 in at least 95% of the
subsets (Epskamp et al., 2018).

```{r stability}
st <- net_stability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
st
```

The reported CS-coefficients are 0.70 for strength and 0.90 for expected
influence. Under the diagnostic's criterion, a drop proportion of 0.70
retains correlations of at least 0.7 with full-sample strength in at least
95% of the sampled subsets. Epskamp et al. (2018) recommend a coefficient
above 0.25, preferably above 0.5, for interpreting centrality. Both estimates
comfortably exceed these reference values. This supports the stability of
the centrality pattern in the example, although it does not resolve every
pairwise difference. The plot displays mean correlations by drop proportion,
with a band showing one standard deviation and a horizontal threshold at 0.7:

```{r stability-plot}
plot(st)
```

## Is the edge structure stable when cases are dropped?

`net_casedrop_reliability()` applies the same case-dropping design to the
edges. At each drop proportion it compares the edge weights of each subset
with those of the full sample through their correlation and through the mean,
median and largest absolute difference. The edge-weight CS-coefficient is
defined as for centrality.

```{r casedrop}
cd <- net_casedrop_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
cd
```

The edge-weight CS-coefficient is 0.90. Mean correlations between subset
and full-sample edge weights are 0.999 after dropping 10% of cases and
0.943 after dropping 90%, suggesting that the overall arrangement of edge
weights is retained across the sampled subsets. This does not mean that
individual estimates remain equally precise. The mean absolute deviation
rises from 0.012 to 0.112 across these drop proportions, while the mean
maximum absolute deviation rises from 0.028 to 0.261. At the largest drop
proportion, appreciable differences in individual edge estimates can
therefore coexist with a high overall correlation.

```{r casedrop-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(cd)
```

## Does the network replicate across halves of the sample?

`net_split_reliability()` divides the sample at random into two halves,
estimates a network on each, and compares the two sets of edges, repeating the
split many times. The result has one row per comparison measure, with its
mean, standard deviation and the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles across splits.

```{r reliability}
rel <- net_split_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
rel
```

Across 100 random 50/50 splits, the mean correlation between the two
sets of edge weights is 0.982. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the
correlations are 0.953 and 0.996. Each half contains 150 observations, but
the halves are repeatedly drawn from the same dataset, not from two new
independent studies. The mean absolute edge-weight deviation across splits
is 0.064, and the mean of the maximum absolute deviations is 0.142. These
results indicate strong agreement in the overall edge pattern within this
dataset, alongside some variation in particular edge weights; they do not
by themselves demonstrate external replication.

```{r reliability-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(rel)
```

## Do the diagnostics apply to other estimators?

Each diagnostic refits the network through `psychnet(method = )`, so it
applies to any estimator. With the unregularized partial correlation network:

```{r pcor}
net_casedrop_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "pcor", iter = 100)
```

The unregularised partial correlation network also has an edge-weight
CS-coefficient of 0.90. Its mean absolute deviations exceed those of the
graphical lasso at each reported drop proportion, reaching 0.139 rather
than 0.112 when 90% of cases are dropped. The absence of regularisation
may contribute to this difference, but these figures alone do not establish
its cause. Each diagnostic also accepts group networks fitted using
`psychnet(..., group = )` and returns results for each group.

## When to use which diagnostic

| Question | Verb | Read the result with |
|---|---|---|
| How precise is each edge and centrality? | `net_boot()` | `as.data.frame(b)`, `as.data.frame(b, what = "centrality")`, `plot()` |
| Do two edges or two nodes differ? | `difference_test()` | the returned table, `plot()` |
| Is the centrality order stable when cases are dropped? | `net_stability()` | `as.data.frame(st, what = "cs")`, `as.data.frame(st)`, `plot()` |
| Is the edge structure stable when cases are dropped? | `net_casedrop_reliability()` | the returned table, `plot()` |
| Does the network replicate across halves? | `net_split_reliability()` | the returned table, `plot()` |

- Report bootstrap intervals for edges of substantive interest. Treat an
  interval containing zero as insufficient evidence to interpret that edge
  confidently, rather than as proof that the relationship is absent.
- Use pairwise difference tests alongside case-dropping stability when
  discussing node rankings. A CS-coefficient below 0.25 warrants particular
  caution about centrality interpretation.
- Distinguish uncertainty in a particular edge from agreement in the network
  as a whole. Here, high case-dropping and split-half correlations coexist
  with two edge intervals that include zero.
- These procedures assume independent observations. For repeated observations
  from the same individuals, resampling must respect the dependence between
  observations from each individual.
